info.name: Zimal Store — Privacy (A5: Erasure & Consent)
info.description:
A5 — GDPR erasure and the consent ledger. BLUEPRINT section 18 (P12, C59-C67).

BEFORE YOU START
1) php artisan migrate
2) keep `php artisan queue:work` running (the emails and audit rows are queued)
3) fill customer_email / customer_password in Variables
4) for folder 5 only: seller_email / seller_password for a user who OWNS an
   open store, plus store_name set to that store's EXACT name
5) run folder 0 first

THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES
GDPR Art. 17 says a person can demand their data be deleted. AML rules say
identity records must be kept for years. Tax law says invoices must be kept
for years. All three are law at once, and any design that honours only one of
them is wrong.

Art. 17(3)(b) is the hinge: the right to erasure does not apply where
processing is required to comply with a legal obligation. So erasure is not
"delete the rows". It is: remove everything that identifies a PERSON, keep
everything the law obliges us to keep, and make sure what is kept can no
longer be tied back to them.

WHAT IS HERE
Folder 0  tokens
Folder 1  the three calls a privacy screen makes to draw itself
Folder 2  consent as an append-only ledger, not a settings screen (P12-5)
Folder 3  what happens when the policy wording changes (P12-6)
Folder 4  requesting erasure, and cancelling during the grace period
Folder 5  C60 - why a store owner has to close the store first
Folder 6  the nightly sweep, with the SQL to see exactly what survived
Folder 7  every expected failure, and why each status code is that code

Folders 3a, 6a and 6c send nothing - they are instructions to read, because
those parts need a .env change or an artisan command. They hit /up so sending
them is harmless.

WARNING
Folder 6 ERASES AN ACCOUNT, irreversibly, and that is the point of it. Use a
throwaway user. Put PRIVACY_ERASURE_GRACE_DAYS back when you are done - 0 days
in production turns a hijacked session from a recoverable incident into a
permanent loss.

NOT LEGAL ADVICE
The retention windows, the 14-day grace period and the consent categories here
are reasonable engineering defaults, not a compliance sign-off. Nothing in this
collection has been reviewed by a lawyer, and the project runs in the UK,
Europe and Pakistan, each with its own rules. Confirm the numbers before
launch.

variable.description: A throwaway user. Folder 6 erases them.
Folder 5 only — must OWN an open store.
Folder 5 only — the EXACT store name, for 5d.
Filled by 1a. Should be DELETE MY ACCOUNT.

request.description:
Fill customer_email / customer_password in the collection Variables first.

This is the PLAIN user — no store. Everything in folders 1-4 and most of 7 runs as this person.
Replace 123456 with the code from the email. The token is saved to {{customer_token}}.

exec: const token = json && json.data ? json.data.token : null;
console.log('No token in response (OTP / 2FA step pending?)');

request.description: ONLY needed for folder 5 (C60 — the store owner). seller_email must OWN an open store.
Saves {{seller_token}}.

exec: const token = json && json.data ? json.data.token : null;

item.name: 1. What the privacy screen reads (safe, read-only)
1a. Erasure status — saves scheduled_for and grace_days

request.description:
Everything a privacy screen needs to draw itself in one call:

  pending              is a deletion already queued?
  scheduled_for        the date the sweep would run
  grace_days           config privacy.erasure_grace_days
  blocked_by           [] when erasure is possible NOW; otherwise a
                       sentence per reason, ready to show the user
  confirmation_phrase  what POST wants typed back (P12-2)
  data_export_url      Art. 15 before Art. 17 — offer the copy BEFORE
                       the deletion, because after it there is nothing
                       left to give them

For the plain customer, blocked_by should be [].

exec: pm.test('Nothing blocks a plain customer', () => pm.expect(d.blocked_by).to.eql([]));

item.name: 1b. My consents — all four types, answered or not

request.description:
Returns every ConsentType, including the ones never answered — a client drawing a privacy screen needs the full list, not only the rows that happen to exist.

Per row:
  granted           is there an active row right now
  version           the wording they agreed to
  current_version   the wording in force today
  needs_reconsent   true when those two differ (folder 3)
  withdrawable      false for terms + privacy_policy (P12-7)
  required          the mirror of withdrawable

exec: rows.forEach(r => console.log(r.type, '| granted:', r.granted, '| version:', r.version));

request.description:
Built earlier, included here because it belongs to the same screen and because it is the thing to click BEFORE asking for erasure.

Streams a JSON file. Deliberately does NOT contain password hashes, 2FA secrets or raw session rows — those are security material, not personal data the user needs handed back, and a leaked export containing them would be a real incident.

201. Writes ONE row: type, the server's current version, granted_at, plus the IP and user agent.

The IP is not tracking — a consent record that cannot say where it came from is weak evidence.

Still 201, and the response is the SAME row. A client re-sending its checkbox state must not pile up a new row every time.

Check in the DB:
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM user_consents WHERE type='marketing' AND user_id=<you>;
It must still be 1.

exec: pm.test('Same version, not a new one', () => pm.expect(d.version).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('marketing_version')));

item.name: 2c. Confirm it reads back as granted

request.description: marketing.granted should now be true and needs_reconsent false.

200. Art. 7(3): withdrawing must be as easy as agreeing was — so this is one call with no password and no confirmation phrase.

The row is NOT deleted. withdrawn_at is stamped on it. Check:
  SELECT type, version, granted_at, withdrawn_at, superseded_at
  FROM user_consents WHERE user_id=<you>;

The row is still there, and it still says we were allowed to email this person between granted_at and withdrawn_at. That is the whole point of the table.

exec: pm.test('Now reads as not granted', () => pm.expect(m.granted).to.eql(false));

request.description:
The AI PRE-CHECK on identity documents specifically — the genuinely optional part.

KYC itself rests on legal obligation, not consent, so withdrawing this does not stop a human reviewing the documents. It only stops them being sent to an automated checker first.
201. This is the row that has to survive erasure (C61) — it is the evidence we were permitted to hold the data at all.
201. Folder 3 uses this one to show version supersession.

item.name: 3a. READ THIS — bump the policy version by hand

request.description:
Nothing to send. This folder needs one change outside Postman.

Run 2g first, then:

1) In .env add or change:
     PRIVACY_POLICY_VERSION=2027-06-01
2) php artisan config:clear
3) run 3b, then 3c.

WHY THIS MATTERS
A consent record is only evidence if it says WHAT was agreed to. When the
policy text changes, the old agreement does not cover the new text — but the
user never refused anything either. Those two states must never be
confusable, so they are different columns:

  withdrawn_at    the user said no
  superseded_at   the document changed under them

Two years later, 'they refused' and 'we rewrote it' have completely
different legal consequences.

item.name: 3b. Read it back — needs_reconsent is now true

request.description: privacy_policy.granted is still true (the old agreement exists), but version and current_version now differ, so needs_reconsent flips to true. That flag is what makes the app show the banner.

exec: console.log('agreed to:', p.version, '| in force now:', p.current_version);

request.description:
201 and a NEW row. Then check the DB:

  SELECT id, version, withdrawn_at, superseded_at
  FROM user_consents WHERE type='privacy_policy' AND user_id=<you>;

Two rows:
  old -> superseded_at set, withdrawn_at NULL
  new -> both NULL, this is the active one

The old row was never touched otherwise. Nothing in this table is ever
updated in place or deleted.

item.name: 3d. P12-6 — a client cannot claim an older version

request.description:
Sends version: 1999-01-01 in the body. It is IGNORED — the request only accepts `type`, and the server records the version currently in force.

Otherwise a client could claim the user agreed to wording it never showed them, which is exactly the kind of record that falls apart under scrutiny.

exec: console.log('client asked for 1999-01-01, server recorded:', d.version);

item.name: 4a. Ask to be deleted — saves scheduled_for

request.description:
202 Accepted, not 200. Nothing has been deleted — a request was recorded and a date was set.

TWO guards on this call, stopping two different mistakes:

  password      stops someone ELSE doing it. A stolen access token is
                enough to READ the account; it must not be enough to
                destroy it.
  confirmation  stops the OWNER doing it by accident. A mis-tapped
                button on a phone cannot type a phrase.

Then check your inbox. The confirmation email is sent NOW, not when the
sweep runs (C65) — after the sweep there is no address left to send to.
It is also the only chance the real owner gets to stop a deletion they
never asked for.

pending: true, requested_at and scheduled_for filled.

Note what has NOT changed: you are still logged in, your profile is intact, your tokens still work. Erasure waits (P12-3).

200. erasure_requested_at is cleared and a second email goes out saying nothing was removed.

That email also says: if it was not you who cancelled, change your password. The grace period cuts both ways.
pending back to false, scheduled_for null. The account is exactly as it was.

item.name: 5. C60 — a store owner must close the store first
5a. READ THIS — what this folder is actually testing

request.description:
Needs {{seller_token}} from folder 0 (B1 + B2), for a user who OWNS an
open store.

THE REASONING
A store is not personal data. It is a trading entity with buyers behind it,
open disputes, tax records, and AML records tied to its identity documents.
Erasing the owner out from under it would leave a live shopfront with nobody
legally behind it.

So the two flows CHAIN, and both halves already existed before A5:

  close the store      Phase 8b
  -> its KYC documents live out their retention window    Phase 9a
  -> then erasure is allowed

Nothing new had to be built to make this correct. The guard just refuses to
let the first step be skipped.

It checks OWNERSHIP, not membership. A manager or staff member owns nothing,
so somebody else's store never blocks their erasure — test that separately
with a staff token if you want to see it.

pending: false, but blocked_by now has one entry:

  "Your store \"...\" is still open. Close the store first, then ask for
   your account to be deleted."

That string is written for the user, not for a log. The UI shows it as-is, which is why the blocker interface returns a sentence rather than a code.

409 Conflict, with reasons[].

409 and not 403 on purpose: the request is LEGITIMATE and will be allowed later. The account is simply in a state that cannot accept it yet. 403 would say 'you may never do this', which is wrong.

Set {{store_name}} in the collection Variables to the EXACT store name first — closing has its own typed confirmation.

This is the step the blocker was insisting on. It also starts the Phase 9a retention clock on the store's identity documents.

exec: console.log('store closed — the retention clock on its KYC documents starts now');

item.name: 5e. Now the same request is allowed -> 202

request.description:
202. Same call, same user, same password — the only thing that changed is the store's status.

Note what did NOT happen: the store's KYC documents were not deleted early. Erasure does not shortcut a legal retention clock; those files go when Phase 9a's window says they go.
Unless you actually want this seller erased on the next sweep, cancel here. The store stays closed; use POST /v1/seller/profile/reopen to ask for it back.

item.name: 6. The nightly sweep (a command, not an endpoint)
6a. READ THIS — how to watch the erasure actually happen

request.description:
There is no endpoint that erases an account. Deliberately: a destructive,
irreversible job belongs on a schedule where it can be reasoned about, not on
a request that a client can fire twice.

  Schedule::command('users:process-erasure-requests')->dailyAt('04:00')

04:00 is AFTER the 03:30 KYC retention purge, so on a night when a closed
store's documents finally age out, they are gone before the owner's account
is anonymised. The two never race.

STEP 1 — nothing is due yet
  Run 4a again (request erasure), then:
    php artisan users:process-erasure-requests
  Expect: 'Erasure sweep: 0 erased, 0 cancelled (blocked), 0 failed.'
  The grace period has not passed, so there is nothing to do.

STEP 2 — make it due
  In .env:  PRIVACY_ERASURE_GRACE_DAYS=0
  php artisan config:clear
  php artisan users:process-erasure-requests
  Expect: 'Erasure sweep: 1 erased, 0 cancelled (blocked), 0 failed.'

  Put the grace period BACK afterwards. 0 days in production means a
  hijacked session is a permanent loss instead of a recoverable incident.

STEP 3 — look at what survived
  SELECT id, uuid, name, email, phone, status, erased_at, deleted_at
  FROM users WHERE id = <that user>;

  The ROW IS STILL THERE (C59). name='Deleted user',
  email='erased-<uuid>@erased.invalid' (RFC 6761 reserves .invalid so it can
  never resolve or receive mail), phone NULL, status inactive, erased_at and
  deleted_at set. The uuid is kept — it is the only handle left and it says
  nothing about anybody.

  Why not DELETE the row? Because audit_logs, user_consents, seller_profiles
  and later orders all point at users.id. A cascade delete here would take
  the audit trail and the consent ledger with it — destroying the very
  evidence that we honoured the request.

STEP 4 — what is gone
  SELECT * FROM user_profiles       WHERE user_id = <id>;   -- empty
  SELECT * FROM user_addresses      WHERE user_id = <id>;   -- empty
  SELECT * FROM user_preferences    WHERE user_id = <id>;   -- empty
  SELECT * FROM user_social_accounts WHERE user_id = <id>;  -- empty
  SELECT * FROM personal_access_tokens WHERE tokenable_id = <id>; -- empty
  SELECT * FROM model_has_roles     WHERE model_id = <id>;  -- empty
  SELECT * FROM seller_team_members WHERE user_id = <id>;   -- empty
  The avatar FILE is gone from storage too, deleted before the row that
  pointed at it.

STEP 5 — what SURVIVED, and why
  SELECT * FROM user_consents WHERE user_id = <id>;
  Still there (C61). These rows are the evidence we were PERMITTED to hold
  the data. Deleting them with the data would destroy the defence for
  everything we did before the request arrived.

  SELECT action, description, new_values FROM audit_logs
  WHERE subject_id = '<id>' ORDER BY id DESC;
  You will see user.erasure.requested and user.erasure.completed.

  Now look closely at new_values on the completed row: id, uuid and a date.
  NO email, NO name, NO phone (C64). Everywhere else in this codebase an
  audit row records old and new values — here it must not, because an audit
  row reading 'erased john@example.com' would put the personal data straight
  back into permanent storage and quietly undo the erasure it was recording.

item.name: 6b. The erased user's old token is dead

request.description:
Paste the erased user's OLD token into {{customer_token}} and send this.

401. Three independent locks had to hold for that: the tokens were deleted, the status cannot log in, and the row is soft-deleted so the login lookup never finds the email. Any one of them failing silently would leave a way back into a 'deleted' account.

item.name: 6c. C63 — a blocker that appears DURING the grace period

request.description:
The one case that is easy to get wrong, and worth reproducing by hand.

Fourteen days is long enough for someone to open a store after asking to be
erased. If the sweep simply skipped them, the request would sit in the queue
forever and nobody would ever be told.

TO REPRODUCE
1) As a plain customer, request erasure (4a).
2) Before the sweep runs, have that user apply and be approved as a seller,
   so they own an open store.
3) PRIVACY_ERASURE_GRACE_DAYS=0, config:clear
4) php artisan users:process-erasure-requests

Expect: 'Erasure sweep: 0 erased, 1 cancelled (blocked), 0 failed.'

  - erasure_requested_at is cleared
  - erased_at stays NULL — nothing was touched
  - an email goes out saying why, so they can ask again once the store is
    closed
  - audit_logs gets user.erasure.cancelled with cancelled_by: 'system'

KNOWN GAP (D6, written in the blueprint rather than hidden)
Nothing currently stops a user with a pending erasure from applying to sell
in the first place. It is not a hole — this re-check catches it — but the
better place to refuse it is the seller application itself. It is recorded,
not quietly widened into this phase.

422 on `password`.

Note this is NOT Laravel's current_password:sanctum rule (C67). That rule calls validate() on the named guard, and Sanctum's guard is a RequestGuard whose validate() expects a 'request' key in the credentials — so it THROWS instead of returning false. The hash is checked directly, which works under any guard.

item.name: E2. Phrase in the wrong case -> 422

request.description:
Sends 'delete my account' in lower case. 422 on `confirmation`.

Exact match on purpose. A phrase that tolerates near-misses stops being a deliberate act.
Password only. Still 422 — both guards are required, neither substitutes for the other.

Run 4a first so something is pending, then send this.

409, and the response repeats requested_at and scheduled_for — so a client that lost track of state learns the date from the error instead of having to ask again.

Cancel with 4c afterwards.

exec: pm.test('The date comes back in the error', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.have.property('scheduled_for'));

request.description:
404. There is no request to cancel.

404 rather than 200: cancelling something that does not exist is almost always a client that thinks the account is in a different state than it is, and silently saying 'fine' hides that.

422, shaped like a field error on `type` so the privacy screen can put the message right next to the toggle the user just tried to turn off.

There is no coherent account that exists while its terms are withdrawn. Asking to withdraw them is asking to close the account, so the API says exactly that instead of pretending to toggle something.
Same reasoning as E6.

item.name: E8. Unknown consent type in the body -> 422

request.description: 422. The enum is the allow-list; anything outside it never reaches the service.

item.name: E9. Unknown consent type in the URL -> 422

request.description:
422, NOT a 500.

It is a route parameter, so ConsentType::tryFrom is used rather than ::from — otherwise an unknown value would be an uncaught ValueError and a raw 500.

200, not an error.

The outcome asked for is 'I do not consent to this', and that is already true. Asking twice for the same outcome is not a mistake, so there is nothing to report. (Run this on a type you have NOT granted.)
401. Every route in this collection sits behind auth:sanctum + active.

401.

Worth noting what is NOT possible anywhere in this controller: there is no {user} parameter on a single route. Everything resolves off $request->user(), so none of it can be aimed at somebody else's account. There is no IDOR surface to test for.
